# pathland-view-core (JVM engine) — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 1, 2026

The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine and runtime for the Pathland protocol.
It owns the `View` SPI and shared authoring vocabulary, the retained-tree
diff emitter, signals/computed/effects, the wire codec, router, cross-platform
state, and JNA ring interop. The Java DSL (`pathland-view`) and the Kotlin DSL
(`pathland-view-kotlin`) are authoring layers over this module; server and
renderer modules depend on core only.

## Implemented

- **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
  `Commands`, `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`, `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`,
  `TokenPath`.
- **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`computed`/`effect`/
  `untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
  caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
  `Scheduler`.
- **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `State`/`PersistentState`,
  untyped `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Generated
  `<View>_StateBinder` classes are loaded from the view's own classloader, so
  application views keep working when a host loads the core in a parent
  extension classloader (Quarkus).
- **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
  `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
- **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
  `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
  `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` stays in the Java DSL because it composes `Button`.
- **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
  `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
- **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
  `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
  Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
  effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
  zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract.
- **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
  `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`, `Configurators`,
  `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
  `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
  wrappers.
- **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
  protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
  `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
  public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
  Java source is generated.
- **Shared engine traces**: `EngineTraceTest` (in `pathland-view`) runs the
  mount/text/property scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under
  `spec/engine-traces/`, byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in
  `spec/ENGINE.md`.
- **Test coverage**: the Java DSL module's test suite exercises the engine
  end-to-end (emitter/reconcile, signals, state, router, transport, JNA ring),
  plus the server/HTML/desktop consumers.

## Package boundary

- `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module for now: `core`/`engine` are logical
  subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
  (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
  `core` and `engine` into separate artifacts requires a node SPI first.
- Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
  `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-test-kit`) depend on
  core, not on the Java DSL. Tests that author views through the DSL add
  `pathland-view` in test scope. The app-facing starters do depend on
  `pathland-view` because application code authors its root `View` with the DSL.
--- view-kotlin ---
# pathland-view-kotlin — implementation status

**Last updated:** November 3, 2026

The idiomatic Kotlin authoring surface (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`). Phase 3 is
complete: every production view/modifier is Kotlin-owned over
`pathland-view-core`; the Java DSL is a test-scope parity oracle only.

## Phase 3

- **Core-owned in Kotlin**: all primitives, shapes, stacks, grids, scroll/lazy
  containers, `ForEach`, `Button`, text/value controls, media, navigation,
  `Label`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`, `ProxyView`, and the complete modifier
  vocabulary (padding/frame/fonts/colors/borders/shadows/effects/transforms/
  interaction/accessibility/environment/styles/window metadata).
- **Dependency boundary**: main depends on `pathland-view-core` only; the Java
  DSL is test-scope for byte-for-byte parity comparisons.
- Tests compare the Kotlin-owned views and modifiers against the Java DSL.

## Implemented

- **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`, `Rectangle`,
  `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`,
  `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
- **Containers**: `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack`, `Grid`, `GridRow`, `ScrollView`,
  `LazyVStack`, `LazyHStack`, `LazyVGrid`, `LazyHGrid`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`,
  `ProxyView`.
- **Controls**: `Button` (title or label subtree), `TextField`, `SecureField`,
  `TextEditor`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `DatePicker`, `Picker`, `Menu`,
  `ColorPicker`.
- **Automatic child collection**: `VStack { Text("a"); Text("b") }` needs no
  `.children(...)`. A custom `KotlinView` constructed inline in a block
  auto-registers; a view stored as a field is added explicitly with `+field`
  inside `body()` (it does not leak into the enclosing scope). An explicit
  `view.add()` / `+view` is available for Java-constructed views (e.g.
  `mediaController.attach()`).
- **Signals**: `signal`, `computed`, `constant`, `effect`, `untracked`,
  `Signal<T>.value`, `WritableSignal<T>.value`, `Signal<T>.map`, `readonly`.
- **Modifier sugar**: `.padding`, `.frame`, `.offset`, `.position`, `.fixedSize`,
  layout priority/z-index/aspect ratio, the full text-formatting surface,
  foreground/background/border/corner radius/shadow, visual effects, transforms,
  visibility/disabled/hit-testing, accessibility, tap/pointer events,
  environment binding, styles, window metadata, and navigation intents. A child
  modifier replaces its auto-registered leaf in the enclosing builder, so
  `VStack { Text("x").fontSize(20f) }` keeps the modifier. The Java
  `.modifiers(...)` operation remains available as an escape hatch.
- **Persisted state**: `KotlinView` base class + `val count by state(0)`
  (auto-keyed by property name) or `state(0, "key")`; a `mutableState(0)` signal
  form for two-way controls. Bound to the session's `PersistentState` before the
  first `body()` render — no kapt and no annotation processor.
- **Reactive bodies**: plain `if`/`when`/`for` in `body()`; `ForEach` over a static
  list or `Signal<List<T>>` with row-scoped child collection.
- **Navigation**: `navigator { route(...) }`, `NavigationStack`, `NavigationLink`,
  `isActive`, and `.navigate`/`.push`/`.replace` intents.
- **Media**: `Video(controller)`; audio remains view-less (`controller.attach()`
  can be added with `+`).
- **Tests**: byte-identical Kotlin-vs-Java frame comparison, auto-collection,
  child-modifier application, modifier property parity, fine-grained signal
  deltas, persisted/stateful bodies, reactive `ForEach`, two-way `TextField`,
  navigation swaps and link intents.

## Not implemented / gaps

- The Kotlin modifier config types (`Padding`, `Frame`, `Border`, `Shadow`,
  `ClipShape`, `Font`) are Kotlin ownership types; code migrating from the Java
  DSL should use the Kotlin `Modifiers` sugar instead of Java config classes.
- A Kotlin-native annotation processor is intentionally not used. `state(...)`
  works on `KotlinView` subclasses; a plain `View` implementation should use
  signals directly or extend `KotlinView`.
- No Kotlin Multiplatform target yet — the module is JVM-only over
  `pathland-view-core`.
- `SecureField` is Kotlin-owned (`TEXT_FIELD` + `IS_SECURE`).

| [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md) | Which **modifiers** (properties) exist and how they encode |
| [EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md) | Which **core events** (raw inputs) exist and how they encode |
| [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) | Golden byte vectors |
| [TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md) | Design-token catalog, resolution, and color-scheme contract |
| **DSL.md** (this file) | How an application **author** composes those into source code |

> **Implementation status** is tracked per implementing project (a `status.md`
> in each protocol crate/library), **not** in this specification. The Java DSL
> (`dev.pathland.view`) and the Rust DSL (`pathland-view`) are the two reference
> realizations; the "Java DSL" / "Rust DSL" columns below record the **agreed
> reference shapes**, not implementation status. This document defines the
> contract only.

### Two guiding rules

1. **Stay as close to SwiftUI as possible.** View names, modifier names, and
  value/min/max, `Border` color+width(+radius), `FixedSize` horizontal+vertical,
  `AspectRatio` ratio+mode, a control's value+range) has **no** shortcut — use the
  lambda. `Padding` is the exception that proves it: its single-value primary is
  `uniform`, and per-edge padding is the lambda.
- **Both forms exist where the member has both**: a raw value and a
  `Signal<T>` (same rule as the config setters above). A two-way control value is
  never a shortcut — it stays a `WritableSignal` config member.
- The Java realization factors both forms through the **single `Modifiers`
  facade**: one `import static dev.pathland.view.Modifiers.*;` brings in every
  lowercase modifier/style function, and each delegates to the same construction
  path (spec §5.6). There is exactly one construction path; the former per-view
  construction `.of(...)` factories and the former per-type `with(...)` overloads
  are **removed** — a shortcut (or the lambda / `.children(...)` / empty `make()`
  for config-less views) replaces every one. Only data/branch factories keep
  `of` (`Color.of`, `Fit.of`, `View.of`, `EnvironmentKey.of`, `Route.of`,
  `Params.of`, `Signals.*`).

Eligible members (non-exhaustive; the companion tables list the surface):

| Kind | Shortcut |
|------|----------|
| Views | `Text(text)`, `Image(source)`, `Icon(name)`, `Label(title)`, `ProgressView(value)`, `RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius)`, `Video(controller)`, `Shape(kind)` |
| Modifiers | `Padding(uniform)`, `FontSize(size)`, `ForegroundStyle(color)`, `Background(color)`, `Tint(color)`, `CornerRadius(radius)`, `Opacity(value)`, `Blur(radius)`, `Rotation(degrees)`, `ScaleEffect(value)`, `LineLimit(value)`, `Kerning`/`Tracking`/`BaselineOffset`/`LineSpacing`/`FontWidth`/`MinimumScaleFactor`/`LayoutPriority`/`ZIndex`(value), `FontFamily(family)`, `HueRotation(degrees)`, `Saturation`/`Contrast`/`Brightness`/`Grayscale`(value), `ColorMultiply(color)`, `ClipShape(shape)`, `AccessibilityLabel(text)`, `AccessibilityRole(role)`, `AccessibilityState(state)`, `Shadow(radius)`, `ImageSource(source)`, `Visible`/`Disabled`/`AllowsHitTesting`(bool), `Underline`/`Strikethrough`(bool), `PointerEvents(mask)`, `TapGesture(action)` |

Per-language adaptation summary:

| Language | Case | Composition mechanism | Example |
|----------|------|-----------------------|---------|
| SwiftUI | `camelCase` | trailing closures + result builder | `VStack(alignment: .center, spacing: 8) { Text("x").padding(16) }` |
| Java (`dev.pathland.view`) | `camelCase` | `make(Consumer)` builder + `modifiers(...)` + `children(...)` | `VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).children(Text.make(t -> t.text("x")).modifiers(padding(p -> p.uniform(16))))` |
| Rust (`pathland-view`) | `snake_case` | assoc fn + `ViewExt` trait + macros | `vstack![text("x").modifiers(Padding(16.0))]` |

---

## 3. State model (signals)

`PathlandSession.setTheme(...)` / `setColorScheme(...)` delegate to the same
emission path. Rust exposes `Engine::reset_theme` / `set_color_scheme` (and
`replace_theme` / `replace_adaptive_theme`).

---

## 8. Java DSL convergence (adopted)

The Java DSL (`dev.pathland.view`) has the complete surface. The convergence
below has been **adopted**: construction through the three operations
(`with` / `modifiers` / `children`), and modifiers as `ViewModifier` values with
**no `Mod` suffix** and **no per-modifier sugar on `View`**. The canonical
contract is [§4](#4-view-surface) and [§5](#5-modifier-surface).

| Canonical | Java (adopted) | Optional / remaining |
|-----------|----------------|----------------------|
| `Text("…")` | `Text.make(t -> t.text("…"))` (String or `Signal<String>`) | — |
| `Button("…", action)` / `Button(action:label:)` | `Button.make(b -> b.title("…").action(action))` and/or `.children(label)` | — |
| `Toggle("label", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.make(t -> t.label("…").isOn(writable))` | — |
| `Slider(value: in:)` | `Slider.make(s -> s.value(writable).min(..).max(..))` (binding in config) | — |
| `.border(color, width)` | `border(b -> b.color(..).width(..))` via `.modifiers(...)` | radius convenience on the same builder |
| `DatePicker(selection:)` | `DatePicker.make(d -> d.mode(..).selection(days))` | *optional* `Date`-shaped config encoding days + millis-of-day per `SET_DATE`/`DATE_CHANGED` |

Adopted conventions:

- **`with` / `modifiers` / `children` are the one construction path.** Every
  concrete view/control exposes these three operations; the former per-view
  construction `.of(...)` is gone (`View.of` is the inline reactive-subtree
  factory, not a view-construction shortcut).
  They are available **at creation or chained, in any order**
  ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)).
- **`make(config)` is a fluent config builder.** The config holds the view's
  values and is the same type a style's `makeBody(Config)` reads
  ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
- **The `View.*` static-factory surface is removed.** The entire factory block
  (`text`, `image`, `rectangle`, `spacer`, `vstack`, `hstack`, `zstack`,
  `button`, `textField`, `textEditor`, `toggle`, `slider`, `stepper`,
  `progressView`, `gauge`, `divider`, `grid`, `scrollView`, `lazyVStack`,
  `lazyHStack`, `lazyVGrid`, `lazyHGrid`, `picker`, `menu`, `colorPicker`,
  `datePicker`, `group`) is deleted from `View.java`.
- **`Group` is a first-class view.** `Group.children(View...)` is a
  transparent container view (SwiftUI `Group`).
- **Core and custom modifiers share one mechanism.** Core modifiers are
  `ViewModifier` values (`padding(p -> p.uniform(16))`,
  `foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(color))`) applied via `.modifiers(...)` —
  there is **no sugar on `View`**; several modifiers at once use
  `.modifiers(...)`, innermost-first. Single-value modifiers pass the value
  directly (`FontWeight.BOLD`).
- **No `Mod` suffix.** A modifier type is named for the modifier it applies;
  where it wraps a single value, the value type is the modifier. Main's
  `FrameMod → Frame` (with the wire batch renamed `emit.Frame → ProtocolFrame`)
  is the precedent; the remaining `*Mod` types are renamed accordingly
  (`FontWeightMod → FontWeight`, `ButtonStyleMod → ButtonStyle`, …;
  `EnvironmentMod → EnvironmentBinding`, `router/NavigationMod → NavigationIntent`).
- **Full `ShapeKind` coverage.** `Circle.make()`, `Capsule.make()`,
  `Ellipse.make()`, `RoundedRectangle.make(r -> r.cornerRadius(..))`, generic
  `Shape.make(s -> s.kind(ShapeKind))` (for `Path`).
- Implementation status: `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`.

---

## 9. Generation contract for a new language

An AI (or a human) generating a Pathland DSL in a new language MUST produce the
following and verify each item. This is a checklist; the authoritative details
are the companion specs.
- **Keep the anchors**: `View`, `Signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `State`,
  `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. These are what make the DSLs
  recognizable; casing and construction follow the host language.
- **`(item, index)` order** for `ForEach`, matching JavaScript `map` and Java
  `BiFunction`; Kotlin/Rust authors may name the lambda parameters.
- **No keys yet.** The emitter reconciles by position + type; a keyed `ForEach`
  is a future protocol/emitter feature, not a syntax difference.
- **Gaps**: Rust reactive-body/`ForEach` parity is Phase 2; the TypeScript plan
  currently defers structural reactivity; Swift is not implemented yet. Kotlin is
  implemented by `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (Kotlin-owned views over core;
  `Text("…")`, `VStack(spacing = 8) { … }`, `.padding(16)`), with its surface and
  gaps tracked in that module's `status.md`.

### 9.4 Conformance recipe

A generated DSL is verified by proving it **emits the same bytes** as the
reference implementations:

1. Port the golden vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) into the new
   DSL's test harness; assert byte-identical `TREE`/`PARAMETER`/`EVENT`/`META`
   opcodes for each canonical element.
2. Port the Java `EmitterTest` cases (mount → `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE`
   deltas; unchanged tree → zero opcodes; two-way routing: `TEXT_CHANGED`,
   `VALUE_CHANGED`, `DATE_CHANGED` write into the bound signal).
3. Verify the no-heap-allocation steady-state property where the target
   language supports it (the Rust engine proves zero dynamic allocations during
   steady-state emission).
4. Cross-check every referenced id against PRIMITIVES.md/MODIFIERS.md/EVENTS.md
   (the specs are the source of truth, never the reference code).

**Reference implementations to read**: Java — `lib/java/pathland-view`
(the DSL: `dev.pathland.view`) + `lib/java/pathland-view-core`
(`dev.pathland.view.core*` + `dev.pathland.view.engine`); Rust —
`lib/rust/crates/pathland-view` + `pathland-engine` + `pathland-core::signal`.

---

## 10. Appendix A: SwiftUI ↔ DSL signature map

Representative rows; the full surface is in [§4](#4-view-surface) and
[§5](#5-modifier-surface).

| SwiftUI | Canonical DSL | Java DSL | Rust DSL |
|---------|---------------|----------|----------|

### Two guiding rules

1. **Stay as close to SwiftUI as possible.** View names, modifier names, and
  value/min/max, `Border` color+width(+radius), `FixedSize` horizontal+vertical,
  `AspectRatio` ratio+mode, a control's value+range) has **no** shortcut — use the
  lambda. `Padding` is the exception that proves it: its single-value primary is
  `uniform`, and per-edge padding is the lambda.
- **Both forms exist where the member has both**: a raw value and a
  `Signal<T>` (same rule as the config setters above). A two-way control value is
  never a shortcut — it stays a `WritableSignal` config member.
- The Java realization factors both forms through the **single `Modifiers`
  facade**: one `import static dev.pathland.view.Modifiers.*;` brings in every
  lowercase modifier/style function, and each delegates to the same construction
  path (spec §5.6). There is exactly one construction path; the former per-view
  construction `.of(...)` factories and the former per-type `with(...)` overloads
  are **removed** — a shortcut (or the lambda / `.children(...)` / empty `make()`
  for config-less views) replaces every one. Only data/branch factories keep
  `of` (`Color.of`, `Fit.of`, `View.of`, `EnvironmentKey.of`, `Route.of`,
  `Params.of`, `Signals.*`).

## 8. Java DSL convergence (adopted)

The Java DSL (`dev.pathland.view`) has the complete surface. The convergence
below has been **adopted**: construction through the three operations
(`with` / `modifiers` / `children`), and modifiers as `ViewModifier` values with
**no `Mod` suffix** and **no per-modifier sugar on `View`**. The canonical
contract is [§4](#4-view-surface) and [§5](#5-modifier-surface).

| Canonical | Java (adopted) | Optional / remaining |
|-----------|----------------|----------------------|
| `Text("…")` | `Text.make(t -> t.text("…"))` (String or `Signal<String>`) | — |
| `Button("…", action)` / `Button(action:label:)` | `Button.make(b -> b.title("…").action(action))` and/or `.children(label)` | — |
| `Toggle("label", isOn: writable)` | `Toggle.make(t -> t.label("…").isOn(writable))` | — |
| `Slider(value: in:)` | `Slider.make(s -> s.value(writable).min(..).max(..))` (binding in config) | — |
| `.border(color, width)` | `border(b -> b.color(..).width(..))` via `.modifiers(...)` | radius convenience on the same builder |
| `DatePicker(selection:)` | `DatePicker.make(d -> d.mode(..).selection(days))` | *optional* `Date`-shaped config encoding days + millis-of-day per `SET_DATE`/`DATE_CHANGED` |

Adopted conventions:

- **`with` / `modifiers` / `children` are the one construction path.** Every
  concrete view/control exposes these three operations; the former per-view
  construction `.of(...)` is gone (`View.of` is the inline reactive-subtree
  factory, not a view-construction shortcut).
  They are available **at creation or chained, in any order**
  ([§2](#2-canonical-signature-notation)).
- **`make(config)` is a fluent config builder.** The config holds the view's
  values and is the same type a style's `makeBody(Config)` reads
  ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
- **The `View.*` static-factory surface is removed.** The entire factory block
  (`text`, `image`, `rectangle`, `spacer`, `vstack`, `hstack`, `zstack`,
  `button`, `textField`, `textEditor`, `toggle`, `slider`, `stepper`,
  `progressView`, `gauge`, `divider`, `grid`, `scrollView`, `lazyVStack`,
  `lazyHStack`, `lazyVGrid`, `lazyHGrid`, `picker`, `menu`, `colorPicker`,
  `datePicker`, `group`) is deleted from `View.java`.
- **`Group` is a first-class view.** `Group.children(View...)` is a
  transparent container view (SwiftUI `Group`).
- **Core and custom modifiers share one mechanism.** Core modifiers are
  `ViewModifier` values (`padding(p -> p.uniform(16))`,
  `foregroundStyle(f -> f.color(color))`) applied via `.modifiers(...)` —
  there is **no sugar on `View`**; several modifiers at once use
  `.modifiers(...)`, innermost-first. Single-value modifiers pass the value
  directly (`FontWeight.BOLD`).
- **No `Mod` suffix.** A modifier type is named for the modifier it applies;
  where it wraps a single value, the value type is the modifier. Main's
  `FrameMod → Frame` (with the wire batch renamed `emit.Frame → ProtocolFrame`)
  is the precedent; the remaining `*Mod` types are renamed accordingly
  (`FontWeightMod → FontWeight`, `ButtonStyleMod → ButtonStyle`, …;
  `EnvironmentMod → EnvironmentBinding`, `router/NavigationMod → NavigationIntent`).
- **Full `ShapeKind` coverage.** `Circle.make()`, `Capsule.make()`,
  `Ellipse.make()`, `RoundedRectangle.make(r -> r.cornerRadius(..))`, generic
  `Shape.make(s -> s.kind(ShapeKind))` (for `Path`).
- Implementation status: `lib/java/pathland-view/status.md`.

---

## 9. Generation contract for a new language

An AI (or a human) generating a Pathland DSL in a new language MUST produce the
following and verify each item. This is a checklist; the authoritative details
are the companion specs.
- **Keep the anchors**: `View`, `Signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `State`,
  `ForEach`, `View.of`, `children`, `modifiers`. These are what make the DSLs
  recognizable; casing and construction follow the host language.
- **`(item, index)` order** for `ForEach`, matching JavaScript `map` and Java
  `BiFunction`; Kotlin/Rust authors may name the lambda parameters.
- **No keys yet.** The emitter reconciles by position + type; a keyed `ForEach`
  is a future protocol/emitter feature, not a syntax difference.
- **Gaps**: Rust reactive-body/`ForEach` parity is Phase 2; the TypeScript plan
  currently defers structural reactivity; Swift is not implemented yet. Kotlin is
  implemented by `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin` (Kotlin-owned views over core;
  `Text("…")`, `VStack(spacing = 8) { … }`, `.padding(16)`), with its surface and
  gaps tracked in that module's `status.md`.

### 9.4 Conformance recipe

A generated DSL is verified by proving it **emits the same bytes** as the
reference implementations:

1. Port the golden vectors in [CONFORMANCE.md](./CONFORMANCE.md) into the new
   DSL's test harness; assert byte-identical `TREE`/`PARAMETER`/`EVENT`/`META`
   opcodes for each canonical element.
2. Port the Java `EmitterTest` cases (mount → `SET_TEXT`/`SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_DATE`
   deltas; unchanged tree → zero opcodes; two-way routing: `TEXT_CHANGED`,
   `VALUE_CHANGED`, `DATE_CHANGED` write into the bound signal).
3. Verify the no-heap-allocation steady-state property where the target
   language supports it (the Rust engine proves zero dynamic allocations during
   steady-state emission).
4. Cross-check every referenced id against PRIMITIVES.md/MODIFIERS.md/EVENTS.md
   (the specs are the source of truth, never the reference code).

**Reference implementations to read**: Java — `lib/java/pathland-view`
(the DSL: `dev.pathland.view`) + `lib/java/pathland-view-core`
(`dev.pathland.view.core*` + `dev.pathland.view.engine`); Rust —
`lib/rust/crates/pathland-view` + `pathland-engine` + `pathland-core::signal`.

state.output:
modifier's property wins).

### The three operations

Every concrete view exposes the same three operations — **construction**
(`make`), **modifiers** (`.modifiers`), and **children** (`.children`). In the
Java realization `make(...)` **is the only static of the three**; a later call
overrides an earlier value for the same property.

| Operation | Purpose | Canonical (SwiftUI-shaped) |
|-----------|---------|----------------------------|
| **values** | Configure structural/layout values and a control's bound value | `View(config:)` — labels in the constructor |
| **modifiers** | Apply `ViewModifier` values, innermost-first | `.modifier(_:)` / `.padding(_:)` / … |
| **children** | Supply the content subtree (content-bearing views only) | trailing closure `{ … }` |

The **canonical builder spelling** (the recommended form; per-language spellings
are in [§9.3](#93-language-adaptation-rules)) is:

```
ViewName.make(values)              // values   — a config-builder lambda (Java views)
      .modifiers(modifier, ...)       // modifiers — varargs
      .children(view, ...)            // children  — varargs, content-bearing views only
```

In the Java realization a view's values entry is the static `make(...)` (the
construction factory; empty `make()` for config-less or value-less starts).
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation available on the builder and on any
`View` value (the interface default), so it (and `children(...)`) chain on the
builder in any order:

```
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).children(a, b).modifiers(m)
VStack.make(v -> v.spacing(8)).modifiers(m).children(a, b)
VStack.make().modifiers(m).children(a, b)
```

The old static `X.modifiers(...)` first-call entry points are **removed** —
`modifiers(...)` is an **instance** operation (interface default for bare `View`
values, covariant override on the builder). Static `X.children(...)` is **kept**
as a value-less first-call convenience (`HStack.children(a, b)` ≡
`HStack.make().children(a, b)`); `make(...)` is the only values static.

**Values are a config-builder lambda.** `make { c in … }` populates a per-view
fluent **config** (`VStack.Config`, `Text.Config`, …). It is the *same type* a
style's `makeBody(Config)` receives ([§5.7](#57-styleable-controls-the-style-contract)).
The builder is **fluent and mutable**: setters return the config. Config-less
views (`Divider`, `Spacer`) take an empty `make()`.

**Every value member is reactive-capable (MUST).** A config member that carries a

Answer format: concise sections.

## What “deployment” means here

In Quarkus, **deployment** does not mean deploying to a server. It means the **build-time / augmentation half of an extension**. Every Quarkus extension is normally a pair:

- **runtime artifact** — `pathland-quarkus` / `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`: the CDI beans, endpoints, and classes used at runtime.
- **deployment artifact** — `pathland-quarkus-deployment` / `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`: build steps Quarkus runs during `quarkus:dev`, test, and package.

The link is generated in the runtime jar:

```properties
# pathland-quarkus/target/classes/META-INF/quarkus-extension.properties
deployment-artifact=dev.pathland:pathland-quarkus-deployment:0.1.5
```

So `dev.pathland.quarkus.deployment` is simply the package holding the Quarkus build-step class.

## What ours currently do

Both deployment modules contain only a feature marker:

- `PathlandProcessor` → `FeatureBuildItem("pathland")`
- `PathlandKotlinProcessor` → `FeatureBuildItem("pathland-kotlin")`

That makes Quarkus recognise/list the extensions (`Installed features: [pathland, pathland-kotlin, …]`). No runtime code generation or bytecode transformation happens.

## Are they still needed?

**`pathland-quarkus-deployment` — yes.** It is the required deployment half of the DSL-neutral `pathland-quarkus` extension. Removing it breaks extension resolution in Quarkus dev/build.

**`pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment` — yes, under the current design.** It is the required deployment half of the separate `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` extension. Removing it while keeping that extension would break Quarkus.

## Possible simplification

Since `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment` has no Kotlin-specific build steps, you could instead:

- turn `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` into a **plain starter/alias POM** (core extension + `pathland-view-kotlin` + `quarkus-kotlin`), not a Quarkus extension, and
- delete `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`.

That would leave only `pathland-quarkus-deployment` and reduce one module. The trade-off is losing the separate `pathland-kotlin` feature listing and the extension’s own descriptor. If no Kotlin build-time integration is planned, the plain-starter approach is simpler.

But is the Kotlin one redundant? Let's inspect extension dependency graph: pathland-quarkus-kotlin depends on pathland-quarkus and pathland-view-kotlin + quarkus-kotlin. It has its own extension descriptor. Since core deployment is a dependency of kotlin deployment, Quarkus will run both build steps: core registers "pathland", kotlin registers "pathland-kotlin". Why both? To expose separate feature names/listings and because each Quarkus extension requires its own deployment artifact/processor. But functionally PathlandKotlinProcessor adds nothing; if the Kotlin extension were just a runtime wrapper, it could inherit core's build steps? Let's think Quarkus extension mechanics: Quarkus discovers deployment modules via runtime `quarkus-extension.properties`. For `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, if it declares deployment-artifact `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-deployment`, that deployment module's build steps + its dependencies' build steps run. It depends on `pathland-quarkus-deployment`, so core feature step also runs. If instead `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` had no deployment artifact and just depended on `pathland-quarkus`, it wouldn't be a Quarkus extension but a normal dependency; core extension would still be discovered transitively and its deployment steps run. So the Kotlin one could be a plain module. But currently both because:

- They correspond to two separate Quarkus extensions: DSL-neutral core and Kotlin DSL convenience.
- Each extension requires a deployment module; each deployment module needs at least one build step? Does Quarkus require a build step class? But they added a FeatureBuildItem for each so Quarkus logs distinct features.

parts.text:
Need answer why both demos exist. Likely historical and different purposes:
- `pathland-quarkus-demo`: original Quarkus demo, Java host, verifies core extension + proxy feature + multiple mounted apps + demo assets + observability; uses shared Kotlin music player + AdView; currently the more complete integration demo.
- `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo`: introduced during Kotlin-first refactor to prove the Kotlin DSL Quarkus extension and Kotlin-only authoring path; also tests Kotlin CDI/all-open and DOM bundle; currently mounts MusicPlayerView (KotlinDemoView commented out). It was designed to not depend on Java DSL/demo views.
With Java DSL gone, the distinction has narrowed: both are Quarkus SSR/WS demos mounting Kotlin views. The main remaining differences:
  - demo1 uses core `pathland-quarkus`, Java CDI beans, multiple mounted apps (/ and /ad), proxy integration, assets route, metrics/logging.
  - demo2 uses `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, pure Kotlin modules/config, all-open, and a smoke test.
  - demo1 has proxy test; demo2 has bundle smoke test.
- Are both still needed? Could be consolidated, but each validates a different extension artifact (`pathland-quarkus` vs `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`). If `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` remains a separate extension, keeping a demo for it is useful as an integration test. Also `pathland-quarkus-demo` validates multi-app/proxy/mounted apps. But if Kotlin extension is collapsed into a plain starter, demos could merge.

Need maybe inspect scripts run commands and CI. `run-quarkus-demo.sh` vs `run-quarkus-kotlin-demo.sh`. Also status. We have enough.

Question maybe implies "why do we still have both after Kotlin-only?" Answer: historical split; currently one demonstrates richer platform features, one proves Kotlin extension. Need recommend consolidation? Since plan mode, can propose options and ask. Could say if goal is to reduce, merge into one Kotlin-host demo using `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, and keep proxy/multi-app in it; then delete `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo` or rename. Or keep both as integration coverage for both extensions.

Need be accurate: `pathland-quarkus-demo` host is Java but views Kotlin; `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo` is Kotlin host. The Java demo also validates Java host mounting Kotlin views (requirement). The Kotlin demo validates Kotlin-only extension/all-open. Since we now require Java host mounting, we shouldn't delete Java demo unless another Java host test covers it. Spring demo still Java host, but Quarkus Java host proof is valuable; `pathland-quarkus` tests also have Java CounterApp mounting Kotlin fixture. So could remove Java demo and rely on tests, but losing proxy demo.

Also `KotlinDemoView` is unused (commented out), so the Kotlin demo currently mounts the shared MusicPlayerView, same as the Java demo. Thus both demos render nearly the same app; difference mostly extension/host/deps and extra Java demo features (ad proxy/assets/metrics). The Kotlin view remains dead code. That's a smell. We can mention.

Could inspect application.properties differences.

# --- Same-server proxy demo (spec/PROXY.md) ------------------------------------
# The music player at / embeds the small ad app mounted at /ad (this same server)
# as a sponsored slot in its Now Playing pane, via a ProxyView. This is the origin
# app's base URL the player proxies; point it at another host/port to proxy a
# remote app instead.
pathland.demo.ad-url=http://localhost:8080/ad

# --- Per-window id on the first request (issue #155) ---------------------------
# Opt the DOM client into the service worker that attaches the per-window id to
# top-level navigations, so the SSR renders the right persisted-state scope on the
# FIRST paint (instead of defaults that the live connection then corrects). The id
# never appears in the URL. Off by default; the worker is served at /_pathland/sw.js
# with Service-Worker-Allowed: / (root scope) and no-cache.
pathland.service-worker=true

# Static resources (the demo's media/icons are served from a disk extraction via
# DemoAssetsRoute, which also sends its own caching headers; this covers the rest
# of Quarkus's static resources, e.g. the DOM client bundle).
quarkus.http.static-resources.max-age=168h

# Pathland SSR debug comments: when true, every rendered HTML node is prefixed
# with a comment naming its component type and the modifiers applied, e.g.
#   <!-- #1 VStack: spacing=4, alignment=Fill -->
# Debugging aid — opt-in; the live /ws deltas are unaffected.
# pathland.debug-html=true

# --- Observability (issue #62) -------------------------------------------------
# Structured (JSON) console logging — the production-shaped reference app default.
quarkus.log.console.json.enabled=true
# Metrics: Micrometer counters/timers at pathland.* are exposed at /q/metrics
# (Prometheus); health at /q/health (smallrye-health). See pathland-observability.
#
# OpenTelemetry spans per frame send / event batch are OPT-IN. The starter wires the
# tracing decorator automatically when a Tracer is available, so to enable them just
# add the extension and point it at a collector:
#   <dependency>io.quarkus:quarkus-opentelemetry</dependency>
#   quarkus.otel.exporter.otlp.traces.endpoint=http://localhost:4317
# (the extension is intentionally NOT a dependency here, so local dev is quiet).

They were added at different times for different purposes, and now overlap heavily.

**History**
- `pathland-quarkus-demo` is the original Quarkus integration demo. It uses the DSL-neutral `pathland-quarkus` extension, is a **Java host**, and is the production-shaped demo: two mounted apps (`/` + `/ad`), same-server proxy, extracted assets route, JSON logging, metrics, and `ProxyDemoTest`.
- `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo` was added with the Kotlin DSL extension (`f697e079` → demo `c67b7f0f`) to prove the Kotlin-only path: Kotlin host, Kotlin CDI/all-open build, `pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, and a DOM-bundle/SSR smoke test.

**Current reality**
- Both mount the same `MusicPlayerView`. The Kotlin demo’s own `KotlinDemoView` is dead code — `newRoot()` returns `MusicPlayerView()` and `KotlinDemoView` is commented out.
- The Kotlin demo’s remaining unique value is build/extension coverage (`pathland-quarkus-kotlin`, Kotlin all-open, Kotlin CDI) plus `KotlinDemoSmokeTest`.
- The Java demo’s unique value is Java-host mounting, multi-app/proxy behavior, assets, and observability.

**Recommendation**
- Keep `pathland-quarkus-demo` as the single reference Quarkus app — it proves the Java-host requirement and exercises the harder features.
- Either:
  1. keep `pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo`, but make it mount `KotlinDemoView` so it actually demonstrates Kotlin-only authoring, or
  2. delete it and rely on the `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` extension tests, or
  3. collapse `pathland-quarkus-kotlin` into a plain starter (then delete its demo + deployment module).

If maintenance cost matters most, option 3 gives one Quarkus demo, one deployment module, and no duplicate full app.

 This document provides essential context for AI agents (or human contributors) working on the **Pathland** protocol. It captures the project's direction, architectural decisions, and implementation details to ensure consistency.

 ## Architecture: Rust Opcode Engine
 
 > The canonical core is a **Rust engine** that emits the application's
 > **declarative view structure** — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing, padding,
 > alignment — as a fixed **16-byte opcode ring buffer** into shared linear
 > memory, consumed by host renderers. View components and modifiers are written
 > in Rust with a SwiftUI-like API, and in Kotlin with the hand-written
 > **`dev.pathland.view.dsl` DSL** (reusable JVM library, Java 17+); both drive the
 > engine through the flat **native C ABI** (`pathland-view-native`) over a
 > zero-copy shared ring on desktop. Java hosts mount Kotlin views through
 > `PathlandApp`.
 
 ### The 16-byte Opcode Engine
 
 - Every opcode is exactly **16 bytes**: `Category (1B) | Command ID (1B) | Flags (2B) | A (4B) | B (4B) | C (4B)`, `#[repr(C, packed)]`, little-endian.
 - A 64-byte cache line holds exactly **4 opcodes** → L1-cache-friendly.
 - Opcodes live in a **ring buffer** in linear memory; the guest writes at `writeCursor`, the host reads from `readCursor`; frame boundaries via a monotonic `frameCount` in the header block.
 - **Both directions are binary**: a second **event ring** (host → guest) carries `EVENT`-category opcodes. The renderer writes raw inputs at `eventWriteCursor`; the guest drains them at `eventReadCursor`. Events are 16-byte opcodes through the engine, never a side-channel callback.
 - **Variable-length data** (strings, token paths) lives in a bump **arena**; opcodes reference entries by offset (`[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`), so every opcode stays 16 bytes. A second host-owned **event arena** mirrors this in the host → guest direction (shared-memory event strings, e.g. `TEXT_CHANGED`); over the network, host → guest strings ride the batch's string section.
 - **Window metadata** (`META::SET_WINDOW_METADATA`, field family `TITLE`/`DESCRIPTION`/`LOCALE`) carries the hosting surface's presentation metadata; renderers map it to their own chrome (browser `<title>`/meta description/`<html lang>`, GTK/Qt window title). It is root-scoped and signal-backed, so a route title is a computed over the router. Web-only artifacts (canonical/robots/sitemap) stay host-owned.
 - Spec: **`spec/OPCODE.md`** (primary) + **`spec/CONFORMANCE.md`** (golden vectors). Companion catalogs: **`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`** (views), **`spec/MODIFIERS.md`** (modifiers/properties), **`spec/EVENTS.md`** (events), **`spec/LAYOUT.md`** (frame & layout allocation contract) — draft IDs are allocated there spec-first.
 
 ### Declarative, not positioned (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The engine describes WHAT the UI is — VStack, HStack, Text, spacing,
 > padding, alignment — never WHERE it is. It does not compute layout and does
 > not emit rects.**
 
 - The engine emits **declarative structure** (`TREE` create/delete/insert/remove/move) + **constraint properties** (`PARAMETER` spacing/padding/alignment/FILL/HUG hints).
 - **Native elements everywhere**: each platform's renderer maps the opcode stream onto that platform's native elements — GTK4 widgets on desktop, DOM elements in the browser, HTML server-side — and those native elements lay themselves out. Never a generic canvas unless a platform has no native equivalent.
 - **Reactive emission**: emission is diff-based. Only the nodes that changed emit opcodes (property diffs via `SET_PROPERTY`/`SET_TEXT`, structural diffs via `TREE` opcodes). An unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes. Signals in the application mark the tree dirty; the engine reconciles.
 - **Zero dynamic heap allocations** during steady-state emission (proven by test).
 
 ### no_std / wasm32 direction guard (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 `pathland-core` and `pathland-view` must remain `#![no_std]` + `alloc` and

 consumer today, but the core must not become desktop-only. Verify with
 `lib/rust/check-wasm.sh` (i.e. `cargo build -p pathland-core -p pathland-view
 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`).
 
 ### Reactive signals (Angular-style)
 
 `pathland-core::signal` provides writable signals that live in the engine. A
 node binds its text (`Node::text_binding`), a property
 (`Node::property_bindings`) or a **string property** (`Node::string_bindings`,
 e.g. a media controller's `MEDIA_SOURCE`) to a `SignalId`; during emit the engine
 resolves the binding and records the dependency, and `Engine::set_signal`
 re-emits **only the bound nodes** (`SET_TEXT` / `SET_PROPERTY`) — no full tree
 walk. Signal values
 are one of `F32`/`U32`/`Bool`/`Enum`/`Str` (packed to the wire's `u32` value or
 arena string). Foreign hosts reach signals via the flat C ABI
 (`pathland_native_signal_create_*` / `signal_set_*` / `node_bind_text` /
 `node_bind_property`) and the Java `Signal` type. Binding then calling `emit`
 records the dependency; a subsequent `set` is a partial emit. (Computed/derived
 signals + effects are the planned next step.)

 ### HTML base design (`design/`)
 
 The HTML renderer's built-in stylesheet is generated from a **three-layer Style
 Dictionary pipeline** plus hand-authored reset/component CSS (one built-in base
 design; no app-facing base-design selection):
 
 ```
 design/tokens/base/*.tokens.json      # internal palette + scales (not emitted)
 design/tokens/semantic/*.tokens.json  # protocol catalog semantics (emitted)
 design/tokens/component/*.tokens.json # per-component surface (emitted)
 design/html/{reset,components}.css    # hand-authored CSS consuming var(--pl-*)
 design/scripts/{build,dev,check}.mjs  # SD build, watcher/preview, validation
 design/build/base.css                 # generated: reset + tokens + components
 design/build/base.css.name            # content hash: base-<sha256-12>.css
 ```
 
 - Tokens are flat DTCG entries (`$value`/`$type`/`$extensions.pathland`) because
   the catalog has both leaf and group paths (`control.border` vs
   `control.border.width`). Dark values live on `$extensions.pathland.dark`;
   durations/z-index/`em` icon sizes are marked internal.
 - `npm --prefix design run build` generates
   `design/build/{tokens.css,manifest.json,base.css,base.css.name}`;
   `npm --prefix design run check` validates catalog coverage, layer direction,
   dark/forced-dark declarations, dimension/`isLengthToken` rules, and the CSS
   content hash.
 - `scripts/sync-design-css.sh` copies the bundle + name to
   `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/assets/` (committed; `--check` fails on
   drift). `css.rs` embeds both with `include_str!` (`builtin_css()` /
   `builtin_css_name()`).
 - The renderer's library default is inline (`render_document`); the linked mode
   (`render_document_linked`, C ABI `pathland_html_render_linked` +
   `pathland_html_base_css[_name]`, Java `renderLinked`/`baseCss`/`baseCssName`)
   emits `{base}/base-<hash>.css`. The Spring Boot and Quarkus starters use it
   and serve the renderer-owned bytes immutable (global + mounted bases); token
   overrides/fit rules stay inline.
 - `scripts/lib.sh` (`build_rust_html`), the Maven `refresh-ide` profile, and CI
   run the design build + sync. Do not edit generated CSS by hand.
 
 ### Native C-ABI shim (`pathland-view-native` + `pathland-core-capi`)
 
 The **desktop/cross-language zero-copy path**: `pathland-view-native` exposes the
 flat world (the flat `builder`/`engine` surface) as `pathland_native_*` C
 functions with a **shared-memory ring** the host driver reads in place. Any
 language that links the dylib (Swift/Java/C# via FFI) calls the flat surface —
 no per-component wrappers — and consumes opcodes zero-copy.
 
 `pathland-core-capi` (`libpathland_core`) is the **minimal ring C ABI** for the
 Kotlin DSL: `pathland_core_create`/`destroy`, `pathland_ring_buffer_push` (one
 raw 16-byte opcode), `pathland_core_arena_alloc`, frame boundaries, zero-copy
 `ring_ptr`/`ring_len`, and event drain/send. The Kotlin DSL
 (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`) binds it with **JNA** (lazily loaded, zero JNI) and
 owns the retained tree + diff emission itself.
 
 ### GTK4 Renderer (`pathland-render-gtk`)
 
 The desktop renderer: a single crate that owns **all** GTK/glib/pango usage and
 maps opcode frames **incrementally** onto native GTK widgets (a retained
 `id → gtk::Widget` map). Both the Rust demo and the Java demo render through
 it — the demos **never call GTK or Swing directly**:
 
 - Rust demo links `pathland-render-gtk` as an `rlib` and calls `GtkRenderer::run(...)`
   with a wake closure.
 - Java demo (`pathland-gtk-demo`) loads `pathland-render-gtk` as a `cdylib` via JNA and
   calls `pathland_gtk_run_ring(ring, on_event, width, height)` over the Kotlin view's
   `libpathland_core` ring; native inputs round-trip as `EVENT` opcodes through the shared
   ring. The renderer **writes** the events and **wakes** the host (no payload); the host
   drains the event ring itself via `pathland_core_drain_events`. Events are never
   delivered through a side-channel callback — they flow through the opcode engine.
   The demo mounts the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (the same shared view the web demos use) with the
   app-driven media contract: the renderer plays the tracks through a direct GStreamer
   `playbin` and reports `MEDIA_*` events back; the demo's web-style
   `/_pathland/assets/...` paths resolve against an extracted local asset root
   (`pathland_gtk_set_asset_root`).
 
 The renderer maps native inputs onto the raw `Event` surface via GTK4
 controllers (`Button::clicked` → pointer up, `EventControllerMotion` →
 pointer move/enter/leave), emitting events through the same `Pump::send_input`
 path.
 
 `pathland_gtk::run` passes an explicit empty argv to GTK (the process command
 line belongs to the embedding host — e.g. the JVM's `-cp`/`-D` flags — and must
 not be parsed as GTK options).
 
 ### Kotlin JVM authoring DSL (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`, in `lib/java/pathland-view-kotlin`)
 
 The **sole JVM authoring surface**. It is the SwiftUI-like DSL shared by desktop,
 Spring Boot, Quarkus, and web apps. Components and modifiers:

-  extending `KotlinView` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a
+  extending `Component` or implementing `View`. **Media is a state object, not a

+- **Persisted state**: `Component` provides `val count by state(0)` (auto-keyed

 ## Project Vision
 
 **Pathland is a cross-platform, cross-language UI protocol** that enables retained-mode UI development with multiple renderer backends. It is **protocol-first**, meaning the protocol specification is the source of truth, not any particular implementation.
 
 **Primary Goal**: Write once, run anywhere - Enable UI code to be written once and deployed across web, mobile, desktop, and embedded platforms through different renderer implementations.
 
 **Status**: The Rust opcode engine (16-byte opcode, ring buffer, arena, diff-based reactive emission) is implemented and tested (`cargo test`). See the Architecture section above.
 
 ---
 
 ## CRITICAL ARCHITECTURAL PRINCIPLES
 
 ### Principle 1: Renderer Statelessness (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The renderer MUST NOT retain application state.**
 
 - Renderers are **pure functions** of the opcode stream: same opcodes → same output
 - A renderer MAY retain its **rendered-output tree** (id → native element + computed layout) for drawing, hit-testing, and event routing — this is a cache of its own output, not state
 - The renderer MUST NOT retain component property values as business state, application control flow, or anything the application can change without emitting an opcode
 - The application owns the canonical retained UI tree
 - The engine emits **deltas only**; the renderer applies them to its native elements
 
 **Violation of this principle is a bug, not a feature.**
 
 ### Principle 2: Command-Based Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol transmits tree mutations as a stream of commands, NOT as serialized trees.**
 
 - Each frame is a **batch of delta commands** describing changes
 - Only **actual changes** are transmitted (diff-based reactive emission)
 - Protocol acts like a **VM instruction stream** / ABI
 - Deterministic, linear decoding without schema lookup or reflection
 
 ### Principle 3: Binary Protocol (NON-NEGOTIABLE)
 
 > **The protocol MUST be binary.**
 
 - Open-source, cross-platform binary format
 - Fixed **16-byte instructions** in a ring buffer shared with the host via linear memory
 - Custom instruction-based bytecode, not schema-driven serialization
 - **Both directions are binary**: tree mutations (app → renderer) AND raw-input events (renderer → app) share the same instruction format, so the wire is language- and platform-agnostic

 ### Opcode Format
 
 Every opcode is exactly 16 bytes:
 
 ```
 [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
 ```
 
 See `spec/OPCODE.md` for the full format, ring buffer, arena, and frame lifecycle.
 
 ### Machine-readable protocol manifest
 
 `spec/protocol.tsv` is the target-neutral ID manifest emitted from
 `pathland_core::constants` by `pathland-protocol-manifest` (`cargo run -p
 pathland-protocol-manifest`). It contains only `kind`, `group`, `name`, and
 `value`; each language binding keeps its own representation and validates or
 reads the manifest. There is no Rust→Java source generation.
 
 The JVM mirror is hand-written and checked by
 `pathland-view-core/src/test/java/.../ProtocolManifestTest`: every manifest row
 must match a Java constant, no extra public numeric constants may exist, and
 `ValueTypes.forProperty` must match `property_value_type`. CI regenerates the
 manifest from Rust and fails on drift.
 
 Engine behavior beyond individual opcodes is specified in `spec/ENGINE.md` and
 enforced by shared self-contained frame traces under `spec/engine-traces/`.
 `pathland-engine-golden` emits them from the Rust engine and the JVM
 `EngineTraceTest` compares its encoded frames byte-for-byte.

 | Category | Value | Direction | Description |

 | TREE | 0x01 | Guest → Host | Node create/delete/insert/remove/move |
 | PARAMETER | 0x02 | Guest → Host | Constraint properties (spacing, padding, …), design tokens |
 | EVENT | 0x03 | Host → Guest | Raw inputs: pointer down/move/up, key down/up |
 | META | 0x04 | Both | Reset, environment, window metadata |

 **Stack**: SPACING=0x0001, ALIGNMENT=0x0002, CONTENT_MARGINS=0x0005

 ### Colors
 
 - Literal colors are **sRGB** with D65 white point, packed as `0xAARRGGBB`
 - A color property may instead carry a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference to a token path
 - Semantic token resolution and theme adaptation are **renderer-owned**
 
 ### Design Token System
 
 **Core Principle**: Application defines intent, overrides, and the theme.
 Renderer defines visual appearance, behavior, defaults, and interaction states.
 
 - The **application owns the theme**: token overrides (base = **light**, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark**) and token references in style properties. Token refs cover COLOR and non-color values (`Length` for spacing/padding/font size/radius/border/frame; `FontFamily.Token` for STRING) in the Rust and Kotlin DSLs.
 - The **renderer owns** default token values (light + dark, the full Tier-1 catalog), token resolution (including explicit `dark.` = forced dark and parent fallback), effective color-scheme detection, interaction states (hover, pressed, focus, disabled), and theme adaptation
 - `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` identifies tokens by **dot-separated string paths** (e.g. `color.primary`, `space.2`) with the standard value-type encoding — there is no separate numeric tokenId system. A `dark.` prefix selects the dark variant (`dark.color.primary`); a `DESIGN_TOKEN` reference whose path starts with `dark.` forces the dark value in either scheme
 - **Runtime theming**: `META::RESET_THEME` clears every app override; a replacement theme is reset + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides in one frame. `META::SET_COLOR_SCHEME` forces `platform`/`light`/`dark`. Both are renderer state — no node is re-emitted. Java: `Emitter.replaceTheme`/`setColorScheme` + `PathlandSession.setTheme`/`setColorScheme`; Rust: `Engine::reset_theme`/`set_color_scheme`.
 - An unresolvable token reference leaves the property **unset** (renderer default), never an error or stale value.
 - The protocol MUST NEVER describe hover styles, click styles, visual transitions, conditional styling, or layout tuning for interaction states
 - **Deferred**: applying per-component tokens to native GTK/Qt leaf control chrome; web parent-path fallback.
 
 The HTML renderer's default token values are generated from `design/` (see
 "HTML base design" above). Full details: [Design Token System](./spec/OPCODE.md#design-token-system)
 and the canonical catalog / color-scheme contract in [spec/TOKENS.md](./spec/TOKENS.md).
 
 ---
 
 ## Implementation Guidelines
 
 ### Adding New Component
 1. Add to `component_type` in `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Implement the component type in `pathland-core` (if it affects the retained tree)
 4. Implement native-element mapping in the target renderer (Goal 3–5)
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Adding New Property
 1. Add to the appropriate property module in `constants.rs`
 2. Document in `spec/OPCODE.md`
 3. Handle the value type in `pathland-core`'s diff emission (if a stack/text/size property)
 4. Implement in each renderer's property application
 5. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Modifying Protocol
 1. Update `spec/OPCODE.md` first (and `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` vectors)
 2. Update `constants.rs` and `pathland-core` encoding/emitters
 3. Run `cd lib/rust && cargo run -p pathland-protocol-manifest` and commit the
    updated `spec/protocol.tsv`
 4. Update the hand-written JVM protocol constants (the Java manifest test fails
    with the exact missing/stale row otherwise)
 5. If emission behavior changed, run
    `cargo run -p pathland-engine-golden -- --emit` and commit the trace fixtures
 6. Verify backward compatibility; update `pathland-core`/renderers + tests
 7. Update the affected project(s)' `status.md`
 
 ### Changing the Wire Format
 - Bump the wire `version` field in `spec/OPCODE.md` and `pathland-core`'s header (currently 1). Pre-release format changes are acceptable while version stays 1.
 
 ### Keeping implementation status updated (MANDATORY)
 
 **The agent MUST keep the per-project `status.md` files in sync with the code.**
 Whenever you land a protocol or renderer change — a new component/property/
 command/event, a new encoder/decoder, a new widget mapping, a new modifier or
 renderer feature, a test that proves new surface — **update the affected
 project's `status.md`** (Implemented / Not implemented / gaps) in the same
 change. The specs (`spec/`) describe the protocol contract only and MUST NOT
 carry implementation status; status lives in `status.md` next to each
 implementing project.
 
 ---
 
 ## Common Pitfalls
 
 ### NEVER Do These
 | Anti-Pattern | Why Wrong | Correct |
 |--------------|-----------|---------|
 | Renderer stores application state | Violates statelessness | Application owns the tree |
 | Engine computes layout / emits rects | Violates declarative model | Emit structure + constraints; native elements lay out |
 | Send full trees | Inefficient | Diff-based reactive emission |
 | String property names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | String component names | Larger payloads | Use numeric IDs |
 | Generic RGB | Ambiguous | Explicitly sRGB |
 | Hover styles in protocol | Renderer job | Define in theme |
 | Heap allocation in steady-state emission | Slow | Preallocated snapshot slab + arena |
 
 ---
 
 ## Project Status

**reactive signals** (`pathland-core::signal` — writable `Signal` values bound to node text/properties, so a signal change re-emits only the bound nodes, reachable from Java via the `pathland_native_signal_*` / `node_bind_*` C ABI), host reader to a native-element description (`pathland-render-gtk`), opcode transport with network-batch encode/decode + time/size batching policy (`pathland-core-transport`), golden conformance vectors (incl. raw-input EVENT and network-batch bytes), typed raw-input event encode/decode, `no_std` builds, zero-alloc steady-state emission, the **bidirectional event ring** (host → guest EVENT opcodes in shared memory, drained by the host via a generic `pathland_native_drain_events` C ABI — the renderer only writes + wakes), the **GTK4 renderer** (`pathland-render-gtk`) with Rust demos that render through it without touching GTK directly, the **native Java library set** — `pathland-view-core` (Kotlin: open `View` interface + shared value/SPI vocabulary, **Angular-parity signals/computed/effects** with synchronous flush, fine-grained retained-tree emitter with **node-level binding effects**, `PLPL` wire codec, router, lazy **JNA ring interop** into `libpathland_core`, cross-platform `StateStore` + **`PersistentState`**) and `pathland-view-kotlin` (the sole JVM authoring DSL: SwiftUI-shaped builders, modifier sugar, property-delegate state, navigation/media helpers, styles), `com.pathland.render.html` (JNA shim over the Rust HTML renderer), `com.pathland.state.redis` (Lettuce `RedisStateStore`) — and the **Quarkus Java demo** (`pathland-quarkus-demo`, a Java host mounting the Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` and Kotlin `AdView`), the **Kotlin-only Quarkus demo** (`pathland-quarkus-kotlin-demo`), and the **Spring Boot** (`pathland-spring-boot-demo`, a Java host mounting Kotlin views) **SSR + WebSocket demos** with per-window persisted `State` (Redis/in-memory — every browser window/tab gets its own UI model and state scope via a `sessionStorage` window id, so two windows never share a session). **`EVENT_LISTENERS`** (any element emits raw events via a u32 bitmask property) and **`onTapGesture`**  ---
 
 ## Quick Start
 
 1. Read this file, `spec/OPCODE.md`, and `spec/ENGINE.md`
 2. Run Rust tests: `cd lib/rust && cargo test` (runs all crates)
 3. Build/test the Java libraries: `cd lib/java && mvn install`
 4. Make small changes, verify they work
 
 ---
 
 ## Pathland Mindset
 
 **Always remember**:
 1. Protocol is King
 2. Renderers are Dumb (execute commands only)
 3. Applications are Smart (generate commands)
 4. Only Changes Matter (transmit mutations / reactive emission)
 5. Binary is Beautiful (efficient, deterministic)
 
 **When in doubt**: Check `spec/OPCODE.md`, the conformance vectors in `spec/CONFORMANCE.md`, and the companion catalogs (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md`, `spec/MODIFIERS.md`, `spec/EVENTS.md`, `spec/LAYOUT.md`), and the reference implementation (`pathland-core`). Ask: "Does this maintain stateless renderers?" "Does this only transmit actual changes?" "Does this describe WHAT the UI is, never WHERE?" "Is this representable as a 16-byte opcode in any language?"

Index: README.md =================================================================== --- README.md +++ README.md @@ -1,269 +1,269 @@ # Pathland > An open UI protocol. Declarative UI — written once in any language, rendered natively anywhere. **Status: proof of concept.** It works end to end and the tests are green, but the wire format and APIs may change before 1.0. [![CI](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/PathlandDev/Pathland/actions/workflows/ci.yml) ## Pathland is a protocol Pathland is first and foremost a **binary UI protocol** — not just a framework, and not a single rendering target. Your view declaration compiles to fixed 16-byte opcodes that any renderer applies to native elements. The wire is the contract: a view written in Java, Rust, C#, or anything else produces the **same opcode stream**, and any renderer can apply it. That makes Pathland **language- and renderer-agnostic**: - **Write the UI once, declaratively.** A SwiftUI-shaped DSL in your language of choice — Java, Rust, C#, anything — describes the same view structure, whatever it later runs on. - **Run it on any surface.** The same view code drives today's server-rendered web and the native GTK4 desktop renderer, and is on track for the browser via WASM, embedded chips (LVGL), and native mobile/desktop (SwiftUI/UIKit, Jetpack Compose, Qt) ([Where it's headed](#where-its-headed)). - **Only changes travel.** The protocol is a stream of tiny binary deltas: an unchanged screen transmits zero bytes, and updates are applied in place. **Server-side rendering is the first surface we ship** — the flagship getting-started path — **not the whole story**. It's the on-ramp that's useful today; the protocol underneath is where the portability comes from. ## See it in action The same shared demo views, rendered by two of Pathland's surfaces — server-side HTML in the browser and native GTK4 widgets on the desktop:

Browser — SSR + live WebSocket deltas
Desktop — native GTK4 renderer
Try the hosted Quarkus demo live: **[pathland.onrender.com](https://pathland.onrender.com)**. ## The flagship path today: SSR The fastest way to replace a BFF + JavaScript-frontend stack. You write the **whole UI in your backend language** — Java, C#, Rust, anything. Pathland renders the first page as server-side HTML, so it appears instantly, then keeps it alive with tiny binary updates over a WebSocket. The result is a smooth, reactive UI — delivered by the backend team, without npm, bundlers, an extra build pipeline, or a separate frontend. ``` You declare the UI in your backend │ ▼ The server renders it (HTML) and owns it │ ▼ Only the things that change travel to the client │ ▼ The client applies them to native elements (60FPS) ``` - **You declare the UI** with a SwiftUI-shaped DSL — `VStack`, `Text`, `Button`, styling — right next to your business logic. - **The server renders and owns it.** The first page is plain HTML (instant paint, SEO-friendly); the server keeps the authoritative copy of the UI. - **Only changes travel.** A click, a signal update, a navigation — the server sends a few tiny binary bytes describing exactly what changed. An unchanged screen sends nothing. The client applies them to real native elements (browser DOM, GTK widgets), so the platform does the layout, animation, and accessibility. ## The whole app Add one dependency and one bean, and you have a working app. **Spring Boot** ```java @SpringBootApplication public class MyApp { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(MyApp.class, args); } @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); } } ``` **Quarkus** ```java @ApplicationScoped public class MyApp implements PathlandApp { public View newRoot() { return new MyHomeView(); } } ``` `MyHomeView` is a Kotlin view — authored once and mounted by any JVM host: ```kotlin -class MyHomeView : KotlinView() { +class MyHomeView : Component() { private var count by state(0) // persisted per session, automatically override fun body(): View = VStack(alignment = HorizontalAlignment.CENTER, spacing = 8f) { Text(computed { "Clicked $count times" }) Button("Click me") { count += 1 } }.padding(24f) } ``` A Java Spring Boot or Quarkus app mounts it without any Kotlin authoring code: ```java @Bean PathlandApp pathlandApp() { return () -> new MyHomeView(); } ``` That's it — SSR at any path, live updates over `/ws`, per-session state. *(Imports omitted: the Kotlin view DSL lives in `dev.pathland.view.dsl`; Java hosts only need `dev.pathland.server.PathlandApp` and a Kotlin view factory.)* ## What it removes Today's server team pays for a BFF, a client-side state model, a SPA framework, and a JS build toolchain — all to render UI the server already owns. Pathland removes that layer: the backend *is* the application. There is no frontend contract to maintain, no client state model, and no JavaScript to write — and the same backend code that serves the web can drive other renderers later. ## Why it's smooth Pathland is built for smooth 60FPS UIs: - **Only changes are sent.** A screen that isn't changing transmits zero bytes. Updates are tiny binary deltas, not re-rendered pages or JSON trees. - **Native elements, not a canvas.** The platform lays out and animates real elements — you get native layout, text rendering, and accessibility for free, whether those elements are DOM nodes or GTK widgets. - **A thin client.** The web client is a small static file that hydrates the server HTML and applies updates in place. No framework, no virtual DOM, no re-render cost. ## The part you don't write The web client is a single prebuilt JavaScript file you copy into your static resources. It's shipped, not maintained — all the real logic lives in your backend. (There's also a native GTK renderer for desktop.) ## Where it runs today - **Web (SSR + live WebSocket deltas)** — Java and Kotlin, with Spring Boot and Quarkus extensions and demos; the flagship getting-started path. - **Native desktop (GTK4 + Qt)** — renderers driven by the same protocol, from the Rust DSL and the shared Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` (`pathland-gtk-demo`, `pathland-qt-demo`). Two surfaces, one protocol — the demos' shared views run under both without a rewrite. ## Where it's headed The SSR path above is the on-ramp — the protocol isn't limited to it. Write the app logic once, run it on embedded, mobile, desktop, and browser. Pathland is an open protocol, so the same code that drives the server-rendered UI today can also run on the device itself: - **In the browser**, the app logic compiles to WASM, writes to a shared buffer, and the main thread is left to rendering alone. - **On embedded devices**, the logic runs on one core while another core renders, with the ring buffer carrying the protocol between them — mapped onto a lightweight UI toolkit like LVGL. - **On mobile and desktop**, the same logic drives native renderers — SwiftUI/UIKit on Apple platforms, Jetpack Compose on Android, Qt and GTK on desktop. Wherever it runs, only tiny binary updates travel across the ring buffer and are applied in place — nothing is re-rendered or serialized, which is what keeps the UI stutter-free, even on small devices. ## Try it Each demo has a one-command launcher in [`scripts/`](./scripts/). Run one from the repository root — it builds its own prerequisites (Rust dylibs, the Java reactor) and launches: | Script | Demo | What you get | |--------|------|--------------| | `./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh` | Spring Boot SSR + WebSocket | http://localhost:8080 | | `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket, Java host + Kotlin views (hot reload) | http://localhost:8080 | | `./scripts/run-quarkus-kotlin-demo.sh` | Quarkus SSR + WebSocket, Kotlin DSL (hot reload) | http://localhost:8080 | | `./scripts/run-rust-gtk-demo.sh` | Rust DSL → GTK4 desktop renderer | a native window | | `./scripts/run-java-gtk-demo.sh` | Kotlin `MusicPlayerView` → GTK4 desktop renderer | a native window | ```bash # e.g. the Spring Boot demo ./scripts/run-spring-demo.sh ``` Notes: - The web demos need a JDK 17+ (the whole stack runs on every LTS from 17). - The GTK demos need the GTK4 + libadwaita system libraries. - On macOS the Java GTK demo hands GTK the main thread automatically (`-XstartOnFirstThread`); Linux needs nothing special.  # pathland-view-core (JVM engine) — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 3, 2026
 
 The shared, framework-agnostic JVM engine and runtime for the Pathland protocol,
 now written entirely in Kotlin. It owns the `View` SPI and shared authoring
 vocabulary, the retained-tree diff emitter, signals/computed/effects, the wire
 codec, router, cross-platform state, and JNA ring interop. `pathland-view-kotlin`
 is the sole authoring layer; server and renderer modules depend on core only.
 Java hosts consume the same API through Kotlin/JVM interop.
 
 ## Implemented
 
 - **Protocol** (`dev.pathland.view.core.protocol`): `Components`, `Properties`,
   `Commands`, `Categories`, `ValueTypes`, `Opcode`, `ValueEncoder`, `WireValue`,
   `TokenPath`.
 - **Signals** (`dev.pathland.view.core.signal`): `signal`/`computed`/`effect`/
   `untracked`, synchronous glitch-free flush, equality suppression, error
   caching/retry, circular-dependency detection, and a thread-safe global
   `Scheduler`.
 - **State** (`dev.pathland.view.core.state`): `PersistentState`, untyped
-  `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Kotlin `KotlinView` state delegates
+  `StateStore`, in-memory store and provider. Kotlin `Component` state delegates
   bind directly before `body()`; the Java `State` field/binder machinery and
   annotation processor are removed.
 - **Transport** (`dev.pathland.view.core.transport`): `ProtocolFrame`,
   `FrameCodec`, `Event`, `EnvironmentData`, `OpcodeSink`, `FrameOpcodeSink`.
 - **Router** (`dev.pathland.view.core.router`): `Route`, `RouteTable`, `Router`,
   `Navigation`, `NavigationContainer`, `NavigationIntent`, `Params`, `Chrome`,
   `NavOp`. `NavigationLink` and the navigation helpers live in the Kotlin DSL.
 - **JNA interop** (`dev.pathland.view.core.ffm`): lazy `PathlandCore` binding and
   `RingOpcodeSink` over `libpathland_core`.
 - **Emitter** (`dev.pathland.view.engine`): `Emitter`, `PathlandNode`, `ViewSlot`,
   `RenderResult`, `InputDispatcher`, `ReactiveValues`, `DateInput`, `MediaInput`.
   Implements mount/id assignment, diff-based reactive emission, node-level binding
   effects, structural reconciliation, fit/media/navigation routing, and the
   zero-opcode unchanged recompute contract.
 - **Shared SPI/values** (`dev.pathland.view.core`): `View`, `ViewModifier`,
   `Configurable`, `ChildrenView`, `Modified`, `ViewBuilder`, `Configurators`,
   `Environment*`, `Platform`, `Theme*`, `MediaController`, `WindowMetadata`,
   `ProxyConfig`, `Color`, `Length`, shared enums, style protocols, and modifier
   wrappers.
 - **Protocol manifest validation** (`ProtocolManifestTest`): the hand-written
   protocol constants (`Components`, `Properties`, `Commands`, `Categories`,
   `ValueTypes`) are checked against `spec/protocol.tsv` — including no extra
   public numeric constants and the full `ValueTypes.forProperty` mapping. No
   Java source is generated.
 - **Shared engine traces**: the Kotlin DSL tests run the mount/text/property
   scenarios against the Rust-emitted PLPL fixtures under `spec/engine-traces/`,
   byte-for-byte. The canonical order lives in `spec/ENGINE.md`.
 - **Tests**: `pathland-view-core` owns the signal, state, frame-codec, and
   protocol-manifest tests; Kotlin DSL tests exercise the emitter end-to-end, and
   the server/HTML/desktop consumers cover their integration paths.
 
 ## Package boundary
 
 - `pathland-view-core` is one Maven module for now: `core`/`engine` are logical
   subpackages inside it, with a few deliberate intra-module references
   (`Color`/`MediaController`/`Modified` materialize `PathlandNode`). Splitting
   `core` and `engine` into separate artifacts requires a node SPI first.
 - Production runtimes/renderers (`pathland-server-core`,
   `pathland-render-html`, `pathland-state-redis`, `pathland-test-kit`) depend on
   core. Java-module tests add `pathland-view-kotlin` in test scope and mount
   Kotlin-authored fixture views; production starters remain DSL-neutral.

@@ -0,0 +1,133 @@
+package dev.pathland.view.dsl
+
+import dev.pathland.view.core.Environment
+import dev.pathland.view.core.View
+import dev.pathland.view.engine.PathlandNode
+import dev.pathland.view.core.signal.Signal
+import dev.pathland.view.core.signal.Signals
+import dev.pathland.view.core.signal.WritableSignal
+import dev.pathland.view.core.state.PersistentState
+import java.util.function.UnaryOperator
+import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty
+import kotlin.reflect.KProperty
+
+/**
+ * Base class for application-authored Kotlin views.
+ *
+ * A subclass declares its subtree in [body]; a signal read there re-renders only this
+ * component (the Java emitter tracks the slot). Persisted state is declared with
+ * [state] / [mutableState] and is bound to the session's [PersistentState] before the
+ * first body render — no annotation processor or kapt.
+ *
+ * Constructing a [Component] inside a builder block auto-registers it, so
+ * `VStack { CounterView() }` needs no `.children(...)`.
+ */
+abstract class Component : View {
+
+    private val stateSignals = mutableListOf<StateSignal<*>>()
+
+    init {
+        // Inline construction (`VStack { CounterView() }`) auto-registers. A view
+        // constructed as a field of another view must not leak into the enclosing
+        // builder scope; it is added explicitly with `+field` inside body().
+        if (!insideAnotherViewConstructor()) {
+            registerChild()
+        }
+    }
+
+    /**
+     * A persisted, two-way state signal keyed by the property name:
+     * `private var count by state(0)` or with an explicit store key
+     * `private var count by state(0, "counter")`.
+     */
+    protected fun <T : Any> state(initial: T, key: String? = null): StateDelegate<T> =
+        StateDelegate(mutableState(initial, key))
+
+    /**
+     * A persisted state signal for code that wants the signal directly:
+     * `val name = mutableState("")` can be passed to `TextField(text = name)`.
+     */
+    protected fun <T : Any> mutableState(initial: T, key: String? = null): StateSignal<T> {
+        val state = StateSignal(initial, key)
+        stateSignals.add(state)
+        return state
+    }
+
+    final override fun renderNode(env: Environment): PathlandNode {
+        env.state()?.let { persistent ->
+            stateSignals.forEach { it.bind(persistent) }
+        }
+        val resolved = body()
+        check(resolved !== this) {
+            "${javaClass.name} must return its subtree from body()"
+        }
+        return resolved.renderNode(env)
+    }
+
+    abstract override fun body(): View
+
+    private fun insideAnotherViewConstructor(): Boolean {
+        val self = javaClass
+        return java.lang.StackWalker
+            .getInstance(java.lang.StackWalker.Option.RETAIN_CLASS_REFERENCE)
+            .walk { frames ->
+                frames.anyMatch { frame ->
+                    frame.methodName == "<init>" &&
+                        frame.declaringClass != self &&
+                        frame.declaringClass != Component::class.java &&
+                        Component::class.java.isAssignableFrom(frame.declaringClass)
+                }
+            }
+    }
+}
+
+/**
+ * A persisted state value. It behaves as a [WritableSignal] so it can be passed
+ * straight to two-way controls; binding to the session store happens before the
+ * owning view's [Component.body] runs.
+ */
+class StateSignal<T : Any> internal constructor(
+    initial: T,
+    var key: String? = null,
+) : WritableSignal<T> {
+
+    private var current: WritableSignal<T> = Signals.signal(initial)
+    private var bound = false
+
+    internal fun bind(persistent: PersistentState) {
+        if (bound) return
+        val storeKey = checkNotNull(key) { "State has no key (declare it with `by state(...)`) " }
+        current = persistent.signal(storeKey, current.get())
+        bound = true
+    }
+
+    override fun get(): T = current.get()
+
+    override fun set(value: T) = current.set(value)
+
+    override fun update(fn: UnaryOperator<T>) = current.update(fn)
+
+    override fun asReadonly(): Signal<T> = current.asReadonly()
+
+    /** The auto-saved persisted value (the signal itself is a [WritableSignal]). */
+    var value: T
+        get() = get()
+        set(value) = set(value)
+}
+
+/** Property-delegate form of [StateSignal]. */
+class StateDelegate<T : Any> internal constructor(
+    val signal: StateSignal<T>,
+) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> {
+
+    operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): StateDelegate<T> {
+        if (signal.key == null) {
+            signal.key = property.name
+        }
+        return this
+    }
+
+    override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = signal.get()
+
+    override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) = signal.set(value)
+}

 # pathland-view-kotlin — implementation status
 
 **Last updated:** November 3, 2026
 
 The sole JVM authoring surface (`dev.pathland.view.dsl`), Kotlin-owned over the
 Kotlin `pathland-view-core`. The Java DSL, its processor, and its Java-only
 Quarkus extension/starter alias are removed.
 
 ## Authoring surface

   containers, `ForEach`, `Button`, text/value controls, media, navigation,
   `Label`, `ViewThatFits`/`Fit`, `ProxyView`, styles (`PlainButtonStyle`,
   `BorderedButtonStyle`, label styles, `NativeVideoStyle`), and the complete
   modifier vocabulary (padding/frame/fonts/colors/borders/shadows/effects/

 - Tests are Kotlin-only; golden engine traces and opcode/property assertions
   replace the former Java-vs-Kotlin parity oracle.

 - **SwiftUI-shaped builders**: `Text`, `Image`, `Icon`, `Color`, `Rectangle`,
   `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Capsule`, `RoundedRectangle`, `Shape`, `Divider`, `Spacer`,
   `ProgressView`, `Gauge`, `Label`, `Group`.
